title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 206: Nature's Sticky Secret: The Science of Dry Adhesion
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 206 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

Nature's Sticky Secret: The Science of Dry Adhesion

Paragraph 1. For more than two thousand years, scientists were puzzled by how geckos climb. Unlike tree frogs, which depend on sticky liquid, or insects that hook tiny claws into rough surfaces, a gecko runs smoothly across wet glass and upside-down ceilings. Even more amazingly, it wastes no energy and leaves zero chemical residue behind. In earlier centuries, thinkers guessed geckos used suction cups or static electricity, until twenty-first-century electron microscopes finally revealed the real answer.

Paragraph 2. Gecko sticking power is purely mechanical and physical. Each toe pad carries millions of microscopic keratin hairs called setae, roughly ten times thinner than a human hair. Each seta splits into hundreds of tiny flat tips called spatulae. When billions of these soft tips touch a wall within less than a nanometre, weak molecular attractions called van der Waals forces pull the surfaces together. Combined across billions of tips, these forces easily hold fifty times the gecko's body weight.

Paragraph 3. However, staying glued permanently to a wall would be useless. As engineer Dr. Ronald Fearing explains, gecko adhesion depends completely on foot direction. When the lizard pulls its foot downward and inward, the hairs flatten against the wall and grip tightly. The moment the gecko curls its toes upward, the contact angle changes and the foot comes off instantly, letting the reptile sprint faster than one metre per second up vertical glass.

Paragraph 4. Copying this natural wonder in factories proved difficult at first. Early artificial tapes made from silicone wore out quickly because their soft plastic hairs clumped together under pressure. Later, biophysicist Dr. Kellar Autumn solved this by growing dense rows of carbon nanotubes on flexible sheets. In lab tests, these patches held heavy loads inside vacuum chambers and below minus one hundred degrees Celsius—conditions where ordinary chemical glues freeze and snap.

Paragraph 5. Dry gecko adhesives now promise breakthroughs across medicine, space, and industry. Surgical researcher Dr. Maria Delgado created biodegradable gecko tape for internal wounds, avoiding metal staples and stitches that can poke tissue and cause leaks. Meanwhile, space engineer Dr. Hiroshi Tanaka built robot arms with gecko pads to catch floating space junk, since suction cups cannot work without air. Engineers also hope to assemble smartphones with dry tape so parts peel apart easily for clean, zero-waste recycling.
